title: Lena and the Cellar
premise: Hospice nurse Paloma Villalobos has spent years recording her dying patients' final nights, believing that documentation keeps grief at a safe distance. When the recordings reveal a second voice—a thing in the cellar of the old group home that answers the backwards-counting with questions—Paloma realizes it has been learning names, including hers. As the harvest moon approaches, she must choose between protecting her found family of coworkers and patients by staying silent, or singing the song's forbidden last verse to bind the voice forever. In the end, she sings alone in the cellar, trading her own invisibility for everyone else's safety, and discovers that being seen was the price—and the gift—of belonging.
about_author: Ulyana Vasquez is a former night-shift caregiver who writes horror rooted in the liminal hours of institutional work. She lives near the coast, where she collects lullabies from strangers and never sings them after dark.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. On her night shift at Marigold House, Paloma records patient Mr. Abernathy counting backwards in his sleep—down past zero into a whisper she can't transcribe. Her documentation ritual is established as both devotion and armor. Emotional beat: quiet unease; the comfort of routine beginning to crack.

chapters.title: Second Voice
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Reviewing the recordings, Paloma hears something answer Mr. Abernathy between counts—a low, patient voice asking questions: Who taught you? Who else knows? She tells no one, telling herself it's interference. Emotional beat: denial sharpening into dread as the voice says her name.

chapters.title: Marigold House
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. We meet her found family: head nurse Devi, orderly Marcus, cook Rosa, and dying resident Elena, who hums an incomplete song. The cellar is off-limits—flooded decades ago, they say. Paloma notices everyone avoids its door without ever discussing why. Emotional beat: warmth and belonging, shadowed by collective silence.

chapters.title: What Elena Remembers
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Elena, lucid at midnight, reveals the staff before her all left 'when the moon got full enough to listen.' The cellar voice was once sung to—a lullaby with three verses, and no one alive knows the last one. Emotional beat: grief braided with responsibility; Paloma's records become evidence.

chapters.title: Questions in the Dark
chapters.summary: POV: alternating Paloma and Marcus. The voice begins speaking through sleeping residents, asking each person what they'd trade to belong. Marcus confesses he heard it during his first week and almost answered. Emotional beat: paranoia infecting the household; loyalty tested by secrets kept 'for protection.'

chapters.title: The Harvest Ledger
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Digging through archived records, Paloma finds a pattern: every autumn equinox, one staff member resigns abruptly—or vanishes from the record entirely. Documentation, her prayer, shows her the house has been paying a tithe. Emotional beat: horror of complicity; her invisibility suddenly feels like survival, not virtue.

chapters.title: Devi's Confession
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. Devi admits she's known for twenty years: the voice grants belonging to whoever answers it, then takes them wholly. The last verse exists only in the memory of someone who heard it sung—and Elena is failing fast. Emotional beat: betrayal dissolving into fierce, frightened solidarity.

chapters.title: Elena's Last Verse
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. On Elena's final night, the voice grows bold, counting the whole house down aloud. Elena, dying, teaches Paloma the last verse in fragments—but warns: sing it with your mouth closed, or you answer too. Emotional beat: tender urgency; a deathbed inheritance.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. The moon rises; the voice opens the cellar door itself and offers Paloma everything she's starved for—family, permanence, being known—if she'll only answer one question. Down the stairs, humming the first two verses to hold its attention, she prepares to give the only answer that matters. Emotional beat: terror fused with resolve; climax begins.

chapters.title: The Song Without Sound
chapters.summary: POV: Paloma. In the flooded dark, Paloma mouths the last verse silently while the voice screams her name, trying to make her sing along. The binding holds—the voice becomes just water, just cold. She walks up into the kitchen where Devi, Marcus, and Rosa wait, finally seeing her fully. Emotional beat: costly triumph; invisibility traded for true belonging.
